facts.fact: The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate announced on Friday 23 October 2026 its rejection of the amendment to Article 51 of the 1991 Criminal Code and of the prime minister's decision to set up the National Mechanism for Combatting Cybercrime.

The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate's Freedom Secretariat publicly rejected Temporary Decree No. 7 of 2026, which extended a Criminal Act provision to electronic and media publishing, and the Prime Minister's 19 October 2026 order forming a National Mechanism to Combat Cybercrime, and called for both to be withdrawn.

note: Journalists facing complaints and proceedings is stated without dates or names, so no punishment recorded; the provision's penalties are a law that punishes speech with no one reported charged under the amendment.

facts.fact: The Sudanese Journalists' Syndicate, through its secretary general Mohamed Abdelaziz, criticised the 2025 amendments to the Informatics Crimes Law as a direct threat to freedom of expression and the press and called for wide consultation before passage.
Access Now says Sudan's government ordered 10 internet shutdowns during exams between 13 and 23 April 2026.
Access Now includes Sudan among places living under indefinite internet and communications blackouts, with testimonies from 2024 to 2026.

Al Jazeera Net reports that the General Union of Sudanese Journalists and the Emergency Lawyers group criticised a temporary constitutional decree amending Article 51/A of the 1991 Criminal Act to cover electronic publishing, the union saying the press was not consulted.

note: The amendment widens an offence to electronic publishing, but no one is reported charged under it.
